title: Lesson 7 - A1.3 Impact of Credible Threat
subject: Information Technology
bigQuestion: What can an organisation lose from a cyber attack?

sections.heading: Credible threats and their impact
sections.text: A credible threat is a realistic risk that is likely to cause harm if it happens, not just a possible or theoretical danger. A cyber threat impact is the damage or loss an organisation suffers when an attack successfully affects its systems, data or operations.
points: Example: customer details are stolen in a data breach, leading to financial losses, legal action and damage to reputation
Losses go far beyond one damaged system: they affect operations, finances, reputation and protected ideas
In most real incidents, MORE THAN ONE type of loss happens at the same time
One ransomware attack could stop operations, bring financial penalties, damage reputation and expose confidential information all at once
Schools, shops and online businesses can all suffer downtime, lost trust and theft of sensitive information

head: Type of loss
What it means
Examples
rows: Operational
The organisation can't run properly until systems and data are restored
Production stops; websites and apps go offline; staff can't access data
Financial
Money lost through disruption, compensation and legal costs
Cash flow problems, lost profits, refunds, ICO fines, legal fees
Reputational
Damage to how the organisation is seen
Loss of trust, negative reviews, lower reputation scores
Intellectual property (IP)
Valuable ideas, designs or information stolen or exposed without permission
A new product design leaked before launch so competitors copy it

sections.heading: Operational loss
sections.text: A cyber attack disrupts the normal running of the organisation. It can't operate properly until systems and data are restored.
points: Manufacturing output: production stops because the systems controlling machines fail
Service availability: websites, apps or customer services go offline
Data availability: staff can't access the information they need to work
Even a short period of downtime can be very expensive, especially for businesses that rely on continuous digital services

head: Kind
What it is
Includes
rows: Organisational
The direct hit to the organisation's finances. Business is disrupted and it becomes a higher risk to insure
Cash flow problems (income slows, costs continue); loss of profits; higher insurance premiums
Compensation
Putting things right for customers and partners who were affected. Not the same as fines
Refunds; payments for exposed data; credit monitoring or identity protection; contractual penalties; discounts or write-offs to win customers back
Legal liability
Action from regulators, courts or others, even after customers are compensated
ICO fines for breaking data protection law; penalty payments; investigation costs; legal fees

sections.heading: Reputational loss
sections.text: Damage to how the organisation is seen after a cyber incident. Unlike financial loss, it's hard to measure directly, but it can have serious long-term effects.
points: Loss of trust: customers, partners and investors lose confidence
Negative reviews: criticism on social media, review sites or the organisation's own platforms
Lower reputation scores: independent rating systems downgrade the organisation
Why it's harder to fix than financial loss: money can be recovered or paid, but trust takes a long time to rebuild, and lost customers may never come back

sections.heading: Intellectual property (IP) loss
sections.text: Intellectual property is an organisation's valuable ideas, designs, inventions and information, such as trade secrets. IP loss happens when these are stolen or exposed without permission.
points: Example: a new product design is leaked online before launch, so competitors copy it and the company loses its market advantage
An NDA (non-disclosure agreement) is a legal contract that stops people sharing confidential information. Your slides ask: is it worthwhile?
Think: an NDA gives legal protection and puts people off leaking, but it can't stop a hacker who has no agreement with you

sections.heading: Case study: British Airways (2018)
sections.text: Attackers stole the personal and payment details of around 400,000 customers. One attack caused all four types of loss:

head: Loss
What happened
rows: Operational
Booking and payment systems were disrupted while the airline responded
Financial
The ICO issued a £20 million fine, plus customer compensation costs
Reputational
Extensive media coverage damaged public trust
Intellectual property
Sensitive internal security information was exposed, possibly weakening future defences

sections.heading: Worked example: the pizza chain
sections.text: A pizza chain normally takes 100 orders per minute, with an average order of £23. Ransomware destroys the data from the last 20 minutes of orders. How much is the operational loss?
points: Orders lost: 100 orders per minute × 20 minutes = 2,000 orders
Value lost: 2,000 orders × £23 = £46,000
Winning customers back: apologise, offer refunds, discounts or free items (the compensation costs from this lesson)
Reputation: customers whose orders vanished may post negative reviews and order from a rival instead

sections.heading: Thinking deeper (plenary)
points: Why is reputational loss often harder to fix than financial loss? Money can be recovered; trust takes years to rebuild
Which loss is most serious? It depends on the business: an online shop can't trade without its systems, while a design company's IP may be worth the most
How are customers affected even if they aren't targeted? They can't use services, their data may be exposed, and they may need to change passwords or watch for fraud

keyIdea: A credible threat usually causes several kinds of loss at once: operational (can't work), financial (organisational, compensation and legal liability), reputational (lost trust) and intellectual property (stolen ideas). The British Airways breach hit all four.
flashcards: Credible threat
A realistic risk that is likely to cause harm if it happens, not just a theoretical danger.
Cyber threat impact
The damage or loss an organisation suffers when an attack successfully affects its systems, data or operations.
Operational loss
When an attack disrupts normal running, so the organisation can't operate until systems and data are restored.
Manufacturing output loss
Production stops because the systems that control machines fail.
Service availability loss
Websites, apps or customer services go offline.
Data availability loss
Staff can't access the information they need to work.
Organisational financial loss
The direct hit to finances: cash flow problems, lost profits and higher insurance costs.
Cash flow problems
Income slows or stops while expenses carry on.
Insurance premiums
What an organisation pays for insurance. They rise after a reported breach.
Compensation
Payments to put things right for affected customers or partners, e.g. refunds and credit monitoring. Not fines.
Contractual penalty
A payment owed when agreed goods or services can't be delivered.
Legal liability
Costs from regulators, courts or others: fines, penalty payments, investigation costs and legal fees.
ICO
Information Commissioner's Office: the UK regulator that fines organisations for breaking data protection law.
Reputational loss
Damage to how an organisation is seen: loss of trust, negative reviews, lower reputation scores.
Reputation score
A rating from an independent system showing how an organisation is seen. It can be downgraded after an attack.
Intellectual property (IP)
An organisation's valuable ideas, designs, inventions and information, such as trade secrets.
IP loss
When valuable ideas, designs or information are stolen or exposed without permission.
Trade secret
Confidential business information that gives a company an advantage, e.g. a recipe or product design.
NDA
Non-disclosure agreement: a legal contract that stops people sharing confidential information.
British Airways (2018)
About 400,000 customers' details stolen; £20 million ICO fine; all four types of loss.
Combined impact
Real incidents rarely fit one category. Serious attacks cause overlapping losses.

quiz.q: What is meant by a cyber threat?
o: A possible attack on computer systems, networks or data that could cause harm
quiz.e: A cyber threat is anything that could attack systems or data and cause harm. A credible one is realistic and likely.

quiz.q: Which is a type of loss an organisation could suffer after a cyber attack?
quiz.e: The four types are operational, financial, reputational and intellectual property loss.

o: An organisation's valuable ideas, designs and information
quiz.e: IP is protected ideas and information, such as product designs and trade secrets.

o: It is realistic and likely to cause harm
quiz.e: Credible = realistic and likely, not just possible.

quiz.q: A factory's machines stop because the systems controlling them have been attacked. Which loss is this?
After a breach, a company's insurance premiums go up. Which kind of financial loss is this?
quiz.e: Higher insurance costs are part of the direct, organisational financial loss.

quiz.q: A company pays for credit monitoring for customers whose data was leaked. This is:
quiz.e: Compensation puts things right for the people affected. It's different from fines.

quiz.q: The ICO fines a company for breaking data protection law. Which kind of financial loss is this?
quiz.e: Fines from regulators such as the ICO are legal liability.

quiz.q: Why is reputational loss hard to deal with?
o: It's hard to measure and has long-term effects on trust
quiz.e: Trust takes a long time to rebuild, and lost customers may not return.

quiz.q: A new phone design is leaked online before launch and rivals copy it. Which loss is this?
quiz.e: Stolen or exposed ideas and designs are IP loss, and the company loses its market advantage.

quiz.q: In the British Airways breach (2018), how much was the ICO fine?
quiz.e: The ICO issued a £20 million fine after about 400,000 customers' details were stolen.

quiz.q: Pizza chain: 100 orders per minute, £23 average order, 20 minutes of orders destroyed. What is the operational loss?
In most real-world cyber incidents, how many types of loss happen?
o: Usually more than one at the same time
quiz.e: Serious attacks cause overlapping losses, like the BA breach, which hit all four.

o: A non-disclosure agreement: a contract to keep information confidential
quiz.e: NDAs legally stop people sharing confidential information, which helps protect IP.

quiz.q: Staff can't open the files they need because the file server has been encrypted. Which operational loss is this?
quiz.e: Data availability loss means staff can't get to the information they need.

quiz.q: How might customers be affected even if they weren't directly targeted?
o: They can't use services, and their data may be exposed
quiz.e: Customers feel the knock-on effects: downtime, exposed data and the need to protect themselves from fraud.

apply.title: Which type of loss?
apply.intro: Read each situation and pick the type of loss it shows. Remember: real incidents often cause several at once.

items.task: A hospital's appointment booking system goes offline for two days after an attack.
items.e: The service can't run until systems are restored: operational loss.

items.task: After a breach, a retailer is fined by the ICO and pays lawyers to handle the investigation.
items.e: Regulator fines, investigation costs and legal fees are legal liability.

items.task: An online shop gives every affected customer a refund and a 20% discount to win them back.
items.e: Refunds and discounts to put things right are compensation.

items.task: A hotel chain gets hundreds of one-star reviews on social media after customers' card details are stolen.
items.e: Negative reviews and lost trust are reputational loss.

items.task: A drinks company's secret recipe is stolen by hackers and sold to a rival.
items.e: A trade secret is intellectual property.

items.task: A small café can't take card payments for a week. Its bills are still due but money stops coming in.
items.e: Income slows or stops while expenses continue: a cash flow problem.

items.task: A car factory's production line stops because the computers controlling the robots are encrypted.
items.e: Machines can't run without their control systems: manufacturing output loss.

items.task: A company can't deliver goods it promised a partner because of an attack, and has to pay the penalty in the contract.
items.e: Your slides list contractual penalties as compensation for agreed goods or services that can't be provided.

items.task: An independent rating site downgrades a bank's security score after a breach.
items.e: Independent ratings downgrading the organisation is reputational loss.

items.task: A ransomware attack stops a delivery firm working, leads to an ICO fine, causes bad press and leaks its new route-planning software. Which losses happened?
o: Operational, financial, reputational and IP: all four
items.e: Like British Airways, one attack can cause every type of loss at once.

items.task: Online store: £800 per hour, offline for 10 hours. What sales were lost?
items.e: £800 × 10 hours = £8,000. Always show your working in the exam.

items.task: After a breach is reported, a company's yearly insurance bill rises by 40%.
items.e: A breach makes the organisation a higher risk to insure, so premiums rise.

pts: A realistic risk that is likely to cause harm if it happens
rather than just a possible or theoretical danger
An organisation's valuable ideas, designs, inventions or information
e.g. trade secrets or new product designs, which give it an advantage
exam.tip: Definition + an example earns both marks.

exam.q: 3. Describe two kinds of financial loss an organisation could suffer after a cyber attack.
pts: Kind 1 named, e.g. organisational financial loss
Description, e.g. cash flow problems, lost profits and higher insurance premiums
Kind 2 named, e.g. compensation / legal liability
Description, e.g. refunds and credit monitoring for customers / ICO fines, investigation costs and legal fees
exam.tip: Use the slides' three kinds: organisational, compensation, legal liability. Name it, then describe it.

exam.q: 4. Explain why reputational loss is often harder to fix than financial loss.
pts: Reputational loss is hard to measure and has long-term effects on trust
so even after the money is recovered, customers, partners and investors may not come back for a long time
exam.tip: Compare the two: money can be recovered, trust takes much longer.

exam.sc: Kestrel Games is a UK games studio with 60 staff. A week before launching its new game, it is hit by ransomware. Its servers are encrypted and its online store is offline for 3 days. The unreleased game's designs are leaked online, and the email addresses and passwords of 50,000 customers are exposed. The online store normally takes an average of £1,500 per hour.
exam.q: 5. Calculate the sales Kestrel Games lost while its online store was offline. Show your working.
pts: Working: 3 days × 24 hours = 72 hours, × £1,500
Answer: £108,000
exam.tip: Always show your working. You can still get a mark even if the final answer is wrong.

exam.sc: Kestrel Games is a UK games studio with 60 staff. A week before launching its new game, it is hit by ransomware. Its servers are encrypted and its online store is offline for 3 days. The unreleased game's designs are leaked online, and the email addresses and passwords of 50,000 customers are exposed. The online store normally takes an average of £1,500 per hour.
exam.q: 6. Explain the operational loss Kestrel Games suffered.
pts: The servers were encrypted and the online store was offline for 3 days (service availability)
so the studio couldn't sell games or work normally until its systems and data were restored, just before a launch
exam.tip: Use the slides' terms: service availability or data availability, plus what it stopped Kestrel doing.

exam.sc: Kestrel Games is a UK games studio with 60 staff. A week before launching its new game, it is hit by ransomware. Its servers are encrypted and its online store is offline for 3 days. The unreleased game's designs are leaked online, and the email addresses and passwords of 50,000 customers are exposed. The online store normally takes an average of £1,500 per hour.
exam.q: 7. Explain two ways Kestrel Games could face legal liability after this attack.
pts: The ICO could fine Kestrel for breaking data protection law
because 50,000 customers' email addresses and passwords were exposed
Kestrel would have investigation costs and legal fees
for responding to the regulator's enquiries and getting legal advice during and after the incident
exam.tip: Also accept penalty payments if Kestrel misses contracted launch dates. Point + reason, twice.

exam.sc: Kestrel Games is a UK games studio with 60 staff. A week before launching its new game, it is hit by ransomware. Its servers are encrypted and its online store is offline for 3 days. The unreleased game's designs are leaked online, and the email addresses and passwords of 50,000 customers are exposed. The online store normally takes an average of £1,500 per hour.
exam.q: 8. Explain how Kestrel's customers could be affected by the attack.
pts: They couldn't buy or download games while the store was offline
Their email addresses and passwords were exposed, so they need to change passwords
and they are at risk of fraud or account takeover, especially if they reused the password elsewhere
exam.tip: Think beyond the company: what do the customers actually have to deal with?

exam.sc: Kestrel Games is a UK games studio with 60 staff. A week before launching its new game, it is hit by ransomware. Its servers are encrypted and its online store is offline for 3 days. The unreleased game's designs are leaked online, and the email addresses and passwords of 50,000 customers are exposed. The online store normally takes an average of £1,500 per hour.
exam.q: 9. Assess which type of loss is most serious for Kestrel Games.
pts: Considers operational loss: 3 days offline and £108,000 in lost sales, but systems can be restored
Considers financial loss: lost sales plus possible ICO fines, compensation and legal fees
Considers reputational loss: 50,000 customers' data exposed damages trust just before a launch
Considers IP loss: leaked game designs let rivals copy them, and the new game loses its market advantage
Compares the losses, e.g. operational loss is short-term, while IP and reputational loss last much longer
Justified conclusion, e.g. IP loss is most serious because the leaked designs can't be taken back and the launch was the studio's main source of future income
exam.tip: Top-grade "assess" = weigh up ALL four types using the scenario's facts, say which is short-term vs long-term, then make a clear, justified choice.
